The Titanic as a Risk Model for IT Projects
How the confluence of factors that sank the Titanic maps neatly onto risk in modern IT projects — and everyday life.
Coding Corgi illustration for the Titanic as a risk model

Hello everyone! Let's talk about risks. I have a model that I use in both my work and everyday life. I'm talking about the Titanic disaster. The plot is well-known, so I won't repeat it here. I'll list several factors that led to the disaster, and you can apply them to IT and everyday life.

The steel used for the Titanic was the best suited for this purpose. When an iceberg ripped through the ship's side, the steel held, but the rivets didn't. It turned out the company was rushing workers to finish the project faster, as every day of construction meant lost profit. For the riveters, the only KPI was the number of rivets per hour. They used additives to soften the steel, making it fit into the holes with a single blow. But that wasn't a problem, after all, the ship is unsinkable.

The company complied with the law and supplied the ship with sufficient life-saving equipment. However, it sacrificed lifeboats for life jackets. And with the space saved, it upgraded the passenger cabins, allowing it to sell tickets at higher prices. In Arctic conditions, a life jacket is a recipe for agonizing death. But why worry about that? The ship is unsinkable.

When the disaster struck, and the chief constructor declared the ship doomed, the decision to evacuate was made in an indecisive manner. Everyone believed too much that the ship was unsinkable.

The situation was compounded by unfavorable weather (calm), an unknown type of iceberg, flaws in the radio protocol, and the crew's lack of preparedness for a real evacuation. No training was conducted because... well, you know why.

I've personally drawn the following conclusions. Disasters happen when several factors converge. That's why I monitor my projects, my loved ones, mentally replaying the possible confluence of negative factors. The Titanic story also taught me that the pursuit of profit, the hellish conveyor belt, usually leads to people fulfilling their plans, but with inadequate quality.

And I always keep in mind that no matter how perfect the Titanic is, it's made of iron — it can sink. It's the same with any IT system, no matter how much you build into it. Without human ingenuity and experience, it will sooner or later run into an iceberg.

P.S. I love to hide jokes in my drawings, referencing pop culture or the nature of the phenomenon being described. If you found one in the previous picture (AI), I hope you'll find one in this one too.
A small JavaScript variable-declaration example that illustrates why attention to detail matters in software development.

Hello everyone! I want my posts to be interesting for people who aren't too closely involved with programming. Today, we'll talk about attention to detail in software development. Of course, so many books have been written on this topic that you could pave the road from Lisbon to Vladivostok with them (there and back). Therefore, I will focus on only one aspect.

To illustrate what I mean, let's look at a JavaScript example. I have seen many times that developers do not notice the difference among the three ways to declare variables: `var`, `let`, and no keyword at all (as in `a = 10`).

The language was created solely to support simple interaction on web pages, and in those distant times, no one could have imagined that hapless language would be used in complex applications in an unnatural way. Fate can be harsh!

Yes, no one could have imagined that an application would include dozens of scripts written by different people who didn't coordinate their actions. And no one could have imagined that all the variables and functions they declared would be loaded into the runtime simultaneously. What could go wrong? For example, several authors declared variables with the same name, made them global (visible from every end of the application), and started manipulating them. The last variable or function loaded on the page wins. But what if the scripts are loaded dynamically? What if an author declared a global variable in one file, used it in another, but an extra JS file (added after the upgrade) with the same variable name exists in between?

So, it's no coincidence that the Corgi dog in the picture is trying to catch global variables (`var`), but it's not very successful. It's best to limit the scope of variables as much as possible (`let` variable). And the best variable is a constant. We'll talk about this next time.
A tongue-in-cheek look back at monolithic architecture — the security, the simplicity, and the Frankenstein that came after.
Coding Corgi illustration of a monolith

Hello everyone! In hectic times, the mind seeks solace in memories. How can one not recall the good old days and monolithic application architecture?

Let's start with security. Application security is currently growing in tandem with functionality. What happened before? An application is installed on a work computer at a facility where unauthorized access is impossible, or on a mainframe where not every employee has access. Today, the number of attack vectors is countless. Beyond the banal theft of passwords through social engineering, we have exotic methods, such as keyboard-click detection via sound and frequency analysis, and even biometric data substitution via an AI-generated identity. I think one day we'll return to locked rooms, one-time passwords on paper, and film photos instead of digital ones to separate fakes from the real thing.

The monolith also made it easier for components to interact with one another. They were all in the same process. There was no need to authenticate for every request to every component, wait for connections, or worry about component failure due to unavailability. Everything was right there, at your fingertips.

The entire product was tested at once, not piecemeal from different vendors, like Frankenstein. And if this Frankenstein suddenly grew a tail in the next release, well, it's impossible to predict how the center of gravity would shift and whether the whole structure would collapse.

Of course, maintaining a microservices architecture requires dedicated people, and as the number of components grows, command centers are required. And so on, with the accumulation of complexity errors and increasing entropy.

Sooner or later, a new team comes along, blames the previous team, product Ragnarok occurs, and the life cycle begins anew.

P.S. Yes-yes, the monolith has its well-known drawbacks, but can we not be boring for a minute and remember the times when we were younger, the sun was brighter, and girls smiled at us for no reason?

AI for Developers: Hype, Reality, and the Economics Behind It
A grounded look at what AI actually does for software developers today — and why business context, developer understanding, and economics still matter.
Coding Corgi illustration for AI for Developers

Hello everyone! Let's talk about AI. I understand this topic is too noisy. And frankly, it's a vast one. So, let's narrow it down and discuss the real help AI provides to software developers. And of course, we'll talk about when we'll all be replaced by machines.

I've heard polarized opinions, ranging from admiration for AI's omnipotence to disparaging ridicule of its stupidity. Let's look at the facts.

AI helps programmers in the following ways: it generates code from prompts, explains what is happening in the program, gives advice, traces simple chains of variable assignments, and searches for something in the code. Quite a lot!

## Five Technical Revolutions

Big things are seen from a distance. Let's jump back a quarter of a century and look at the tools my colleagues and I had at our disposal. Specifically, in my experience, I used DOS (not Microsoft) and later MS-DOS until Windows 95 was introduced. The text editor for programs was little different from today's Linux console. At best, it was something like Norton Commander with pseudo-graphics and an abundance of hotkeys. Of course, there was no code highlighting or command prompting whatsoever. Debugging tools were rudimentary, essentially printing variable values to the screen.

I remember my admiration for the Borland Delphi development environment (~1999-2000; are you aware of the Y2K problem?). It was my first visual editor that suggested command completions and (oh my god!) could generate the visual interface code sections. In a few clicks (the mouse already worked!), I could create a desktop application with buttons and drop-down lists and launch it. Is that similar to today's AI?

I remember my confusion: if a machine can create a stub application on its own, perhaps it's not worth getting involved in IT, because soon it will be able to write the rest itself?

And now, a quarter of a century later, we're back at the same point. Machines are great at generating code, but they're not capable of fully creating software. Why is that?

At the core of a business are its business processes. Software developers negotiate with business owners (or their representatives), seeking to determine which processes can be automated and what measurable benefits this will yield for the business. Often, business owners themselves can't precisely articulate these processes. Furthermore, any organization has politics, budgets, conflicts of interest, and external factors that aren't included in the model (as a reminder, a smart machine is based on a statistical model). Let's not forget about data access permissions within comprehensive security systems, legacy applications, and other technical issues.

How is an AI supposed to figure this out, negotiate with everyone, and create a comprehensive solution? Huh? It appears easier to build a business from scratch using an AI-native approach.

## Developer's understanding

Another aspect is the software developer's understanding of what they're doing. I prepared a JS file and ran various sorts on it. I can send you the program, as LinkedIn doesn't allow file attachments.

A trivial task? Not exactly. Solution quality depends not only on the data size but also on how the data is distributed within the array; speaking more broadly, what is the data? The execution result shows how much the number of iterations and the time spent differ. You might ask, why do we need an array when we have powerful databases?

In databases, sorting and searching don't happen magically; they follow similar algorithms that take optimization into account. It's not for nothing that we have, for instance, clustered indexes and binary indexes (and other tools). I believe this topic deserves a separate post — one that explains it simply.

It's obvious in the JS file that the AI doesn't see the style issue. The code for shuffling arrays was copied rather than put into a function. A human wouldn't have missed it.

## Economy

Finally, the economic aspect. Please share in comments the names of profitable companies whose business is exclusively related to AI. Its development requires an insane amount of resources. What will this mean for us, the end users? Will they twist our arms with subscription prices in the long run, because we are enterprise users and can pay much more than ordinary users? Or, worse yet, will the costs be hidden in the price of the traditional cloud services we use anyway? I recall the case in which Yandex (a tech giant) switched from Oracle to PostgreSQL in 2016 because "Oracle licenses cost as much as the Golden Bridge."

Even as a tech lead, I face a hypothetical choice: hire a supremely skilled programmer with an orchestra of AI agents or a regular development team. On the one hand, it's cheaper to pay one person, but what if they leave the company and no one else can manage the orchestra? Or what if a task arises that can't be solved through agents? For example, integration with a large and complex system. It seems to me that in "marathon", a team looks more reliable.

## In Conclusion

I have a calm, non-reverent attitude toward AI technology as it applies to our work. It's a useful tool that I use alongside other, time-tested ones. Today, AI is certainly not the Holy Grail and doesn't do our work for us.

What do you think?

Frostpunk: A Survival Simulator That Teaches Hard Leadership Lessons
What the strategy game Frostpunk teaches about resource scarcity, hope, and the uncomfortable trade-offs of leadership.

Hello everyone!

Too-to-do-too-too-too-do-to!

Do you hear music?

Let's dive into the world of computer games we love! I'll kick things off with the strategy game "Frostpunk."

## The Setting

The story unfolds in an alternate history. In 1886, the British Empire was experiencing unprecedented advances in steam technology. A global environmental catastrophe occurs, and the world literally freezes over. The government builds gigantic furnaces in the Arctic. A small group of people, led by the Captain, reaches one of these furnaces. They must survive the harshest conditions, and you, the Captain, must lead them through these challenges.

## Survival Under the Storm

This game isn't entertainment, but a simulator of a small group in extremely harsh conditions. The temperature will constantly drop from a "comfortable" -20°C to -70°C. Moreover, after six weeks, the Storm will hit the valley. The temperature will drop to -120°C, making it impossible to even leave the shelter. Anyone will immediately freeze to death. The player (Captain) must prepare for the Storm.

People start without resources, shelter, food, or technology. Every hour of delay in decision-making leads to defeat. There are never enough people, not enough coal, wood, or medicine. The Captain must decide where to assign people, how to resolve intra-group conflicts, and how to anticipate potential future problems.

You have to send children into the mines, hang dissenters, and mix sawdust into their soup to make it through another day. Typically, you choose between bad and worse.

I've lost many times. But it's not how many times you fall, but how many times you get back up that counts.

The game offers several scenarios. I'll focus on just one.

## The Fall of Winterhome

In "The Fall of Winterhome," you inherit a fragile city recovering from mutiny, with a dying furnace and an evacuation vehicle to prepare.

This scenario teaches players to mix truth and lies to people in a sophisticated way: that the furnace can be fixed, that there's enough room on the transport for everyone, and that you (specifically you) and your family will definitely be evacuated. And when people no longer believe the lies, players need to have trusted people with batons on hand. I've tested it: if you tell people the truth, anarchy quickly ensues. Doomed people quit their jobs, while others try to capture the evacuation vehicle. In short, the success depends on maintaining hope for as long as possible.

Next, a player needs to decide whom to evacuate and carefully remove them from the city's economy to prevent the city's collapse. And no, it's not women and children. Children will die on their own if they aren't accompanied by qualified adults. This is also what the game teaches: the life of an adult in a critical situation is more important than the life of a child.

## The Final Act

When the transport departs, the drama's final act begins. The remaining people in the ruins of the city live out their last days. They try to turn up the heat to survive for a few more hours, but ultimately, the ruins are strewn with frozen corpses.

The game vividly illustrates the well-known saying, "We can afford to be democratic as long as we have plenty of food and women."

Book Recommendation: "The Culture Map" by Erin Meyer
A must-read for anyone working in a multicultural team — Erin Meyer's eight-scale framework for understanding cross-cultural collaboration.
Coding Corgi illustration for The Culture Map

I highly recommend Erin Meyer's "The Culture Map: Breaking Through the Invisible Boundaries of Global Business." The author presents an eight-scale framework that helps you pinpoint where different cultures sit on important dimensions: communicating (low- vs. high-context), evaluating (direct vs. indirect feedback), leading (egalitarian vs. hierarchical), deciding (consensual vs. top-down), trusting (task-based vs. relationship-based), disagreeing (confrontational vs. non-confrontational), scheduling (linear vs. flexible), and persuading (principles-first vs. applications-first).

The book helps us understand each other better. In one culture, giving feedback directly is normal; it's a sign of honesty and respect. Meanwhile, in another culture, it's considered very rude, especially if it happens in public rather than one-on-one.

The same goes for decision-making. For some people, decisions are set in stone — immutable. For others, decisions are fluid and subject to change. Can you imagine what would happen if two such cultures collided? The author provides specific examples.

In short, if you work in a multicultural environment, this book is a must-read.
Why volatile AI vendor pricing pushes me toward building tools with AI rather than relying on agent orchestration.
Coding Corgi illustration for AI pricing

"We are standing on the shoulders of giants"… and borrow their lamps [and ideas].

Actually, I'd like to draw attention again to the extremely volatile pricing policies of AI vendors. Of course, the market itself is still in its infancy, so nothing else can be expected.

Vendors encourage the creation of multi-agent systems. However, agent usage has been billed separately, which adds an extra fee to the cost of use. Keep in mind that vendors can raise prices for enterprise clients at any time.

Therefore, in my opinion, as an engineer, it makes more sense to create tools using AI and use them instead of agents. Because you only pay tokens to create the tool once, and then it works for free (and yields predictably). Meanwhile, using a subagent requires a constant extra fee.

P.S. We, business, and the vendor have conflicting interests in this regard. We need reliable, affordable solutions whose prices we can predict over the long term, while the AI vendor needs to sell us as many tokens as possible.
